articles.text: The special delivery system goes into effect on Oct. 1, in every post-office in the United States. Hitherto, only first and second-class post-offices, were special delivery offices but after Oct. 1, as said, the rule applies to all offices, large or small. The post-office under this system, guarantees the immediate delivery of letters upon which an extra ten cent stamp is affixed.
articles.summary: Announces that special-delivery mail service extends to every U.S. post office on Oct. 1.

articles.text: The United States is placed in a rather embarrassing position in its present difficulty with Mexico. To begin with, the man Cutting, whose arrest has caused the difficulty, is such a notorious fraud that the trouble has many of the elements of a farce. In the second place, a war between the United States and Mexico, would be such an exaggerated case of "big dog eat little dog," that the Government will probably decline to begin a war from very shame. The honor of the nation is at stake, however, and it compels her to demand satisfaction from Mexico for an outrage on even such a citizen as Cutting. Altogether, the affair is so perplexing that it has caused Secretary Bayard to fall into a state of chronic exasperation.
articles.summary: Editorial comment on the Cutting affair dispute between the United States and Mexico.

articles.text: Mandan and Bismarck were visited Sunday afternoon by a violent wind storm which lasted for three hours and did considerable miscellaneous damage. In Mandan, the worst damage was done to George Peoples' building, the tin roof being blown off and furniture, walls, carpets etc., being soaked with water; the total amounting to about $1,500. The Northern Pacific bank building, the new court house and many others buildings were damaged. Probably the whole will amount to $5,000 in Mandan. In Bismarck, the loss is estimated at less than $2,000. The Tribune's signal service report states that the wind blew forty-eight miles an hour. July 13, 1883, it blew fifty-six miles an hour as it did also on April 22 of the same year. On April 18, 1876, was the hardest storm Bismarck has probably ever experienced, the rate at that time being seventy-four miles an hour. The storm of Sunday extended far into Minnesota and altogether did about $25,000 worth of damage.
articles.summary: A Sunday wind storm caused about $5,000 damage in Mandan and under $2,000 in Bismarck.

articles.headline: Abraham Lincoln.
articles.text:
Among recent facts of literary and popular interest, is the announcement of a new illustrated biography entitled "The Every-Day Life of Abraham Lincoln," written by "Those who knew him." The plan of the work is that of an exhaustive biography, giving not only the general facts of his life in chronological order, but incidents, anecdotes and every day facts minutely personal, such as could only be given by those in closest intimate and confidential relations, during the various periods of his life. These were, in pursuance of the plan, enlisted for the work, embracing those who knew him as a boy, as a flatboatman, a rail-splitter, a clerk in a country store, a law student, a lawyer, politican, President—every period of his eventful and most interesting life. Each author writes of the facts of his life during the period in which he knew him—facts and incidents that came under his own observation and within his own knowledge. A book thus written, and so exhaustive in fact concerning one of so enduring a place in the hearts and admiration of his people, is assured of an enthusiast welcome and a lasting place in popular esteem. We are told that the last literary work performed by the late Judge David Davis, Lincoln's lifetime friend, was one of the many contributions to this volume, in which he took a deep personal interest.

It is a grand career and character that is thus so minutely delineated. What lover of simple worth and homely virtues is not touched by the story of Lincoln's pure and manly life? In what other country could it have been possible to produce a character and career like his?

The work is rendered further attractive by nearly 100 superb engravings from original designs made especially for this book, illustrations scenes and incidents in his life. It is sold at popular prices within the reach of all.

The canvassing agent for such a work will find the latch-string out; a welcome and patronage that will make his business both pleasant and profitable. N. D. Thompson Publishing Co., St. Louis, Mo., and New York City, are the enterprising publishers.
articles.summary: Book notice for "The Every-Day Life of Abraham Lincoln," published by N. D. Thompson Publishing Co.

articles.text: Destructive storms were more prevalent last Sunday than any day this year. In many parts of Dakota, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, Indiana and Illinois, great damage was done.
articles.summary: Reports widespread destructive storms across the Northwest last Sunday.

articles.text: Our proposal last week of H. R. Lyons name as a member of the Legislature, has met with the unqualified approval of many of our citizens. We do not know whether Mr. Lyon will run for the office but after a careful canvass of the field we are able to think of no one who would give more general satisfaction. We do not wish to place Mr. Lyon in a wrong light if he does not wish to run, and if he does not, we hope his Mandan friends will make him see the error of his ways, and represent the district in the able, common-sense way for which his business education qualifies him.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy renews its proposal of H. R. Lyon of Mandan as a candidate for the Legislature.

articles.headline: The Territory Deserted.
articles.text: The Indian Territory, said Colonel Taylor in reply to a question, had been lost sight of almost as a cattle country, or rather that portion which was formerly so prominent and gave so much cause for discussion; the Cheyenne and Arapahoe reservation. The cattlemen had shown no disposition to break over the orders of the government in reference to those sections and now a traveller can ride a day in either one of the reservations without seeing more than a dozen cattle. Numerous outfits have been sent in to gather up the stragglers and now there were very few left. The Choctaw and Cherokee strip still offered very good ranges and there also were probably 100,000 cattle on the Comanche grounds, but they gave no trouble and no fear was entertained that they would be removed. Some of the cattlemen who had herds on the strip in the name of squaw men; thus grazing their cattle at less cost than if they leased direct from the Nation; experienced a great deal of trouble on account of an order made by the Nation taking away some of the rights of the squaw men, directing that they should take no herds except on payment of $3 a head. But that trouble was settled by the cattlemen acquiescing, where they had to, on the real owners of the herds becoming known to the Indian officials.—[Globe-Democrat.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Globe-Democrat on cattle being cleared from the Cheyenne and Arapahoe reservation in Indian Territory.

articles.headline: Artesian Wells in Dakota.
articles.text:
In the construction of artesian wells the experience of the pioneers is of value to those who have yet to solve the problem. The true artesian vein is a white sand rock, which lies, at Yankton 600 feet below the surface. Northward from this point the depth of this rock increases, and the in Alexandria neighborhood it probably lies not less than 700 down. To reach the artesian basin it is necessary to pass the drill through chalk, shale, stiff clay, iron pyrites, quicksand and various conglomerates, most of the formations being difficulty to overcome and requiring patience, skill and experience on the part of the well maker. Every foot of the distance between the surface and the water-bearing rock should be tighly cased and it will be found that heavy salt water casing is the most economical in the end, though it is more expensive than the lighter grades. Perfect casing is the most important part of the work. If a portion of the bore is neglected the artesian water when reached sends a considerable portion of its volume off through the loose overlying formations and the defcet is created which constantly increases in magnitude. In searching for the true artesian vein numerous minor veins are generally encountered which produce flowing wells. The discharge from these veins is much less than from the lower veins, and an inferior quality of water is given forth. So it is best to resist the temptation to stop when a tolerable flow is encountered and go down to the artesian sand rock, which has never yet failed to give a spouting well. In the city of Yankton and in its suburbs there are now telvew flowing wells. These vary in depth from 350 to 600 feet. In only the deepest of these was the white sand rock vein reached, and that one is yielding water of the best quality at the rate of 1,500 gallons per minute. the others have a flow of from 30 to 100 gallons per minute. Most of the smaller wells were made for private use and answer the purpose for which they were constructed. But for public uses the deepest is the only one of the dozen which gives a satisfactory flow.

There is reason to believe that almost every Dakota village, city and farm can enjoy the luxury of a spouting well.—[Press and Dakotaian.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Press and Dakotaian on drilling artesian wells in Dakota, citing Yankton's twelve flowing wells.

articles.headline: Two Wonderful Horses.
articles.text:
The wonderful two-year-old Tremont has had a remarkable career. He has started twelve times, and has never been forced to anything like an exertion by the best horses that have been pitted against him. He has won his owners in stakes and purses this year something over $30,000, and will duplicate that amount before the end of the season. He cost $1,600 as a yearling. This splendid colt is jet black, and the only mark on him is a little white star in the forehead, about as big as a silver half dollar. The youngster seemed to be proud of the attention shown him, and moved about the stall, occasionally coming up to take a nip at his master's coat sleeve.

"He is the greatest two-year-old that ever lived," said Captain Conner, and both the Dwyers nodded assent. Philip said: "Yes, he can beat any horse now on the turf for three-quarters of a mile and carry just as much weight as his competitor. He is a good disposition horse also."

Miss Woodford is, in many respects, the most phenomenal race horse I ever knew of. The fact is, she is the only one I have ever known that was just as good at six years old as three. It is really singular how she holds her power.

The splendid mare came up to her master, rubbed her nose against him lovingly, and there was such a beam of intelligence in her eye that it almost seemed as though she understood the praise her owner was giving her and the depth of the admiration he has for her. As he patted her long and beautifully-arched neck Mr. Phil. Dwyer said:

"She has won us $150,000 in stakes and purses—what is known in racing parlance as public money. No race horse in this country has ever yet equalled her performances—that is, been beaten so few times in an equal number of starts."
—[Philadelpha Times.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Philadelphia Times on the Dwyer brothers' race horses Tremont and Miss Woodford.

articles.text: The case of the Territory vs. Joseph Meyer, for horse-stealing, came before the grand jury at Mandan and they failed to find an indictment against him, the evidence not being sufficiently strong. Judge Francis, however, ordered the prisoner held in bonds of $1,000 to the next grand jury, as he learned that the evidence was deemed insufficient because "Calamity" Joe. was accused of stealing the horse from an Indian.
articles.summary: The Mandan grand jury did not indict "Calamity" Joe Meyer for horse-stealing, but Judge Francis held him for the next grand jury.

articles.text: The hail-storm Friday afternoon was almost unprecedent in violence for half an hour, but its track was so narrow that beyond broken window glass the damage was slight. Its path extended but a mile or two north and south of Medora, by ten miles west and twenty east. An immense body of water fell at the same time. Sixty-eight panes of glass were broken out of the Northern Pacific hotel and others suffered in proportion.
articles.summary: A violent Friday hail storm broke windows in Medora, including sixty-eight panes at the Northern Pacific hotel.
